newsitem.title: UK: Sterling/mark falls victim to profit-taking.
newsitem.headline: Sterling/mark falls victim to profit-taking.

text.p: Sterling fell victim to profit-taking after setting new 59-month highs for four consecutive trading days amid expectations of higher UK interest rates.

The pound shed more than two pfennigs, dipping below 2.86 marks at one point, as traders locked in gains they have made as a result of its 2.3 percent surge against the mark in the past week. A widening in UK's trade deficit also undermined sterling.
Traders aren't looking for the pound to fall too far, though, as rate rise expectations remain intact.
"Technically, sterling was looking overstretched after the long move up," said Ian Morris, international economist at HSBC.
"But the fundamentals still look good for sterling and the pullback we have seen is nothing more than a blip in the uptrend."

Sterling/mark was at 2.8689/99 at 1045 GMT from 2.8728/38 late Tuesday in Europe. Cable was at $1.6652/62 from $1.6643/48 yesterday. The pound's trade-weighted index was at 101.4, up from 101.3 earlier in Europe but down from 101.9 Tuesday.

Expectations that UK interest rates are poised to rise have bolstered the pound in recent days. Traders have also been revising up their forecasts of how much rates will rise as evidence of strong consumption mounted up last week.

Rate rise hopes were bolstered after Bank of England Governor George said Tuesday that UK domestic demand was growing at a rate which could not be sustained for long without stoking inflation. Traders are now looking for the newly formed Bank of England's monetary policy committee to raise rates from 6.5 percent when it meets July 10.
"It's easy to see why sterling has come all this way given the strong data and interest-rate expectations," said Marian Bell, treasury economist at Royal Bank of Scotland.
Sterling has also gained from concern that the European single currency will be weak, George said yesterday.
While sterling is expected to resume its rally in the coming days, the toll its gains are taking on UK exporters may prove to be the pound's undoing further out.

Sterling has rallied more than 20 percent against a trade-weighted basket of 20 currencies tracked by the Bank of England. This has eroded British export competitiveness and the value of their foreign-currency earnings.

"If the squeals from the exporters show up in trade data, sterling could come off," said Bell at RBS. UK exporters do not, however, expect sterling to sustain these levels and are waiting to convert their overseas earnings at better rates, she said.

Trade numbers earlier Tuesday briefly weighed on sterling as they showed the UK's global trade deficit widened to 961 million pounds in April, above economists expectations of a 625-million-pound shortfall, from 671 million in March.
Also, the UK's trade deficit with countries outside the European Union widened to 563 million pounds from a revised 425-million-pound gap in April.

Sterling's fate now lies in the hands of Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown, analysts said. Expectations of rate rises will be scaled back if he tightens fiscal policy sufficiently in his July 2 budget.
"If tax rises hit consumers then if will defuse pressure to raise rates and be negative for the pound," said Morris at HSBC. "If not, the weight of managing the economy will fall on monetary policy."
